#10353. Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers

Over the past few years, scaling dense language models has driven most progress in LLMs. From early models like the original ULMFiT (~30M parameters) or GPT-2 (1.5B parameters, which at the time was considered "too dangerous to release" 🧌), and eventually to today’s hundred-billion–parameter systems, the recipe was simple:

More data + more parameters gives better performance.

Scaling laws reinforced this trend, but dense scaling has practical limits:

This is where Mixture of Experts (MoEs) enter the picture.

If you're already familiar with MoEs and want to jump straight into the engineering work done in transformers, you can head directly to Transformers and MoEs.

A Mixture of Experts model keeps the Transformer backbone, but replaces certain dense feed-forward layers with a set of experts. An “expert” is not a topic-specialized module (e.g., "math expert", "code expert"). It is simply a learnable sub-network. For each token, a router selects a small subset of experts to process it.

Different tokens activate different experts, based on their hidden representations.

Model capacity depends on total parameters, but inference speed depends on active parameters.

For example, take gpt-oss-20b. It has 21B total parameters, but uses 4 active experts per token, out of a total of 32 experts. Considering the shared components plus the active experts, this model uses ~3.6B active parameters per token. Running this model on an M3 Ultra Mac, which has a memory bandwidth of about 800 GB, we could estimate generation speed as ~ 800 / (3.6 * 2) in bfloat16, where each parameter takes 2 bytes. This yields about 111 tokens per second. The actual performance number we get is ~115 tok/s, which is very close to the back-of-the-envelope calculation.

This super fast speed confirms the model works approximately as a 3.6B parameter one, but it has the same capacity (or quality) as a 21B parameter model.

(Note: speed would be even faster if we used kernels for the native mxfp4 quantization the model uses).

Given a fixed training FLOP budget, MoEs often outperform dense counterparts.

This means faster iteration and better scaling efficiency.

Experts provide a structural boundary in the computation graph. Since different tokens engage different experts, we can parallelize across experts (we discuss this later in Expert Parallelism).

Recent major MoE releases of open models that happened in the past few weeks include Qwen 3.5, MiniMax M2, GLM-5, or Kimi K2.5.

The trend accelerated after the success of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025, building on earlier systems like DeepSeek V2. Another early MoE was Mixtral-8x7B, released in December 2023.

Closed labs use MoEs too. ChatGPT has long been rumored to use a sparse architecture, and the open gpt-oss models certainly do.

If you want to learn more about MoEs in general, we strongly suggest reading this blog and watching our recent YouTube video on routing.

Most tooling in the ecosystem, including model loading, device placement, quantization, and backend execution was originally designed for dense models. MoEs challenge these assumptions.

Making MoEs first-class citizens in transformers means redesigning parts of the loading pipeline, execution model, and distributed abstractions, not just adding new model classes. We’ll focus on how the transformers library has evolved to support sparse architectures across:

AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("model_id") downloads and loads model weights into a PyTorch model. For dense models, loading is relatively straightforward where each tensor in the checkpoint maps one-to-one to a parameter in the runtime module.

For MoEs, it’s more complicated. In most MoE checkpoints, each expert is serialized independently. If you peek inside the DeepSeek-V3 checkpoint index, you’ll see keys like:

Each expert has its own set of weight matrices, essentially 256 (0 to 255 total, taking DeepSeek-V3 as an example) small feed-forward networks saved side by side. At runtime, however, GPUs execute optimized kernels. Modern MoE kernels such as grouped GEMMs and fused MoE implementations are designed to process all experts in a single operation, not by looping over them one at a time.

To do that efficiently, they require expert weights to be packed into a single contiguous tensor.

Bridging this gap systematically is what the weight loading refactor enables.

With the introduction of a generic WeightConverter, the mental model shifted from:

A checkpoint already matches my runtime layout; loading is mostly a key-by-key copy.

A checkpoint is just a serialized source of tensors. Loading is a conversion pipeline that transforms them into the runtime layout we want.

The central abstraction introduced by this refactor is dynamic weight loading via a WeightConverter.

Primitive operations (chunk, concatenate, etc.) are composable. Two that are particularly useful for MoEs:

MergeModulelist merges a list of tensors into a single tensor. For example, you can compose MergeModulelist with Concatenate to stack the experts in a MoE and pack them into one tensor.

SplitModulelist splits a tensor back into a list of tensors. For example, you can split a stack of experts back into individual experts.

The refactor improves not just what conversions exist, but how they’re scheduled.

The loader scans checkpoint keys once, matches them against converter patterns, and groups tensors per converter. Once a key is identified as needed, it’s registered as a future and materialized via a thread pool. Conversion operations run only once their dependencies are ready. For example, MergeModulelist waits until all experts for a layer are loaded.

This avoids repeated scans and reduces memory peaks.

To evaluate the improvements introduced by the new weight-loading pipeline, we benchmarked the v4 vs v5 versions of transformers. The focus is on loading speed of large MoE models, which is often a bottleneck in training and inference.

HF_ENABLE_PARALLEL_LOADING: Enables parallel shard loading via threads.

HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD:Disables the new async pipeline (v5 escape hatch).

Model: Qwen/Qwen1.5-110B-Chat GPU: 1× A100 (80GB)

It’s the combination of Single-pass routing, Async materialization, and Conversion-aware scheduling which together avoid unnecessary materialization and memory peaks while enabling expert packing and projection fusion at load time.

With this refactor we can now create the runtime module structure first and then convert the weights into the structure. We can now optionally attach quantization within the conversion pipeline, making quantization part of the weight loading pipeline itself. This is crucial because quantizing “per expert” only makes sense once experts exist in a predictable packed layout.

This end to end pipeline was not possible earlier and now it comes to the users as an exposed API.

Once experts are packed into a single runtime tensor, another question arises:

How do you actually route through them efficiently?

In a Mixture of Experts model, each token is routed to different experts. This means the runtime must dispatch tokens to their selected expert weights, execute the projections efficiently, apply the routing weights and then collect and reorder the results.

This is what the Experts Backend system (introduced in PR #42697) addresses. The Experts Backend introduces a pluggable execution architecture that decouples expert computation from the model implementation. Instead of hardcoding one dispatch strategy inside each MoE model, the system allows expert layers to dynamically select a backend at runtime.

This is implemented via a decorator pattern:

The decorator wraps expert classes and dispatches computation to the selected backend automatically.

eager which loops over the selected experts and applies projections per expert. This is used for correctness reference and debugging.

batched_mm uses the torch.bmm API. This duplicate selected expert weights per token and performs a single batched GEMM. This backend is very well suited for small batch, GPU-heavy workloads where memory is available.

grouped_mm uses torch._grouped_mm API. Here we sort tokens by expert ID, group them, and then perform a single grouped GEMM. This backend shines with large batches or memory-constrained setups.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) models can have hundreds of billions of parameters (far more than what fits on a single GPU). Expert parallelism (EP) addresses this by distributing experts across multiple devices. Each device loads only its assigned subset of experts, computes for those experts and then participates in result aggregation. This approach scales models to far larger parameter counts without increasing computation cost because each token activates only a few experts.

Expert parallelism is enabled via enable_expert_parallel:

Where N evenly divides the total number of experts, and possibly matches the number of GPUs in your node.

When enable_expert_parallel=True, the model switches from the standard tensor-parallel (TP) plan to an expert-parallel (EP) plan with specialized sharding strategies.

GroupedGemmParallel: This splits the expert weights along the expert dimension (dim=0). Here each device loads only num_experts / num_devices.

RouterParallel: This remaps global expert indices to local indices, masks out experts not assigned to the current rank, ensures each device computes only with its local experts and uses an all-reduce to combine partial outputs across devices.

MoEs are excellent for scaling inference, but training them is significantly more complex.

MoEs have a Massive parameter count, the distributed expert communication is complicated, there are routing in-stabilities that need to be handled. To address this, we collaborated with Unsloth to enable significantly faster Mixture-of-Experts training:

We leverage the Expert Backend abstraction, standardize around PyTorch’s torch._grouped_mm API and use custom Triton grouped-GEMM + LoRA kernels. Unsloth builds on top of the Transformers (and TRL) optimizations to push performance further.

For full details, we recommend reading: Unsloth’s official guide

As sparse architectures continue to evolve, we want the transformers library to evolve with them. If you’re building with MoEs or experimenting with new sparse ideas, we’d love to hear from you. Let us know what abstractions, kernels, or workflows you’d like to see next in transformers.

The enable_expert_parallel flag hiding the complexity of GroupedGemmParallel + RouterParallel behind a single config is a great DX win — distributing experts across devices used to require a lot of custom plumbing.

AI-generated images are becoming an important part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product visuals, blog illustrations, backgrounds, and other digital content. However, creating an image is only the first step. Preparing it for efficient web delivery is equally important.

Unoptimized images can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay page rendering. These problems can affect Core Web Vitals, especially Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques, including image resizing, modern formats, Node.js automation, responsive delivery, and performance testing.

Images often represent a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. When developers upload large images without processing them, visitors may experience slower loading times, particularly on mobile networks.

Large image files that take longer to download.

Incorrect dimensions for different screen sizes.

Missing image dimensions that cause layout shifts.

Excessive compression that reduces visual quality.

Unnecessary downloads caused by poor responsive configuration.

A consistent optimization workflow helps address these problems while maintaining the intended visual appearance.

Before preparing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width hero banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small article illustration.

These are suggested dimensions, not fixed requirements. The actual size depends on the website layout and the devices being supported.

When preparing source visuals, developers can compare different AI image tools to understand how image generation workflows handle aspect ratios, output dimensions, and visual details.

Regardless of the generation method, keep an original high-quality version. This master file can be used to create smaller versions without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Choosing an appropriate image format can reduce file size while maintaining acceptable visual quality.

AVIF: Provides efficient compression for many photographs and detailed illustrations.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and environments requiring broad compatibility.

PNG: Suitable for screenshots, lossless graphics, and images that require transparency.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare the resulting file sizes and inspect image quality before selecting a format.

For technical details, consult the MDN Web Docs guide to image file formats.

Manually resizing multiple images can become time-consuming. Automation provides a consistent way to generate different image dimensions and formats.

Sharp is a Node.js library that supports resizing, compression, and image conversion.

The script generates WebP and AVIF versions at several widths.

The quality values are starting points. Adjust them after checking the output for compression artifacts, loss of detail, and unnecessary file size.

For additional configuration options, refer to the official Sharp documentation.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on available resources and screen layout.

The HTML srcset attribute provides multiple image candidates, while sizes describes the expected rendered width.

The browser uses the available image candidates and layout information to select a suitable resource.

Make sure the sizes attribute accurately reflects the actual website layout. Incorrect values can cause browsers to download larger images than necessary.

Responsive delivery is particularly useful when the same visual appears in different layouts across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide alternative image formats with a fallback.

The browser selects a supported source, while the img element provides fallback behavior and alternative text.

Always verify that the referenced files exist and that their dimensions match the intended layout.

Images without defined dimensions can cause page content to move while resources are loading. This can negatively affect Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Include width and height attributes whenever possible:

The browser can use the dimensions to reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

Images below the initial viewport can also use native lazy loading:

However, avoid lazy-loading the main hero image when it contributes to LCP. Important above-the-fold images should be loaded promptly.

Reducing file size should not significantly affect the visual details required by the website.

This is particularly important for images containing:

A practical quality-checking process includes:

Compare the optimized image with its original version.

Inspect the image at its actual display dimensions.

Test the output on mobile and desktop screens.

The smallest file is not necessarily the best option. A slightly larger image may provide noticeably better visual quality.

After implementing the optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Open Chrome DevTools and select the Network panel. Filter requests by images and reload the webpage.

Mobile devices receive appropriately sized images.

The browser downloads unnecessary image files.

Modern formats are being served correctly.

Important images load without unnecessary delays.

Image dimensions match their display requirements.

You can inspect the image source selected by the browser using:

For websites containing multiple images, inspect each relevant element.

Finally, run an audit using Google PageSpeed Insights. It can help identify oversized images and other performance issues.

The web.dev guide to optimizing LCP also provides useful technical guidance for diagnosing loading delays.

Remember that image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, and JavaScript execution can also influence page loading.

Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

Assuming one image format always provides the best compression.

Using incorrect responsive image settings.

Lazy-loading important above-the-fold images.

Ignoring the actual image selected by the browser.

Measuring file size without checking visual quality.

A proper testing process helps identify these issues before they affect visitors.

No. AVIF often provides efficient compression, but results depend on image content, encoding settings, and quality requirements. Comparing both formats is the best approach.

Four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

Yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

No. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Important images near the top of a webpage should generally load promptly.

The fundamental optimization techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, generated visuals may contain complex textures and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

AI-generated images can improve website design, but efficient delivery requires more than simply exporting and uploading a visual.

Choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive delivery. Include image dimensions to prevent layout shifts, prioritize important visual elements, and test the results across different devices.

By following these practices, developers can maintain visual quality, reduce unnecessary downloads, and create faster, more reliable website experiences.

Anthropic's recent move to have Claude Code deny video game cloning and possibly reverse engineering efforts has come under heavy fire from the software development community. Hot on the heels of Friday's report on the matter, an Anthropic employee responded to the tweet with the purported rule update with a direct statement confirming that the firm added guardrails to Claude Code to prevent game recreation.

In the full tweet, which you can read below, Addy Osmani says that "[Anthropic] added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against [its] usage policy." He goes on to state that work on original games is meant to continue working, and that Anthropic is iterating on the rules to try and "strike the right balance."

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.October 30, 2026

There's no telling what those sentences might be, though given Osmani's choice of words, it's possible that said sentences are indeed what X user Chasm posted a screenshot of: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

In our previous report, we had already linked to recent issues raised at Claude Code's own GitHub repository, comprised of users complaining that the AI assistant was refusing to work on their games or on reverse-engineering tasks. As far as we can ascertain, it appears the game-related blocking is limited to the combination of using Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model. Should that prove true, then users should be able to sidestep the limitation by calling upon Opus using another harness like Ollama or forwarding specific requests through a wrapper of some sort.

Regarding the blocking of reverse engineering, we have received direct confirmations. The first comes from our own alumnus Jarred Walton, who was trying to run checks on the software he's developing. He notes that such work had been performed with no issue until yesterday, October 31, and that switching to Opus 4.8 let him continue his work.

Walton theorizes that Anthropic may have added a new rule to Code specifically for reverse-engineering. Considering that timing, plus the fact that other reports of refusals all popped up around the last week, may indicate that the company could be fiddling with cybersecurity-related rules in the same manner as they are for video game-related content.

We also received screenshots from a staffer's direct acquaintance, who asked Opus 5.5 (via Code) to try and reverse engineer a product activation, a request that likewise triggered safeguards. Meanwhile, notices that Claude Code appears to block reverse-engineering continue to mount, now with a Redditor allegedly having their account suspended, and then reinstated, over using Opus 5.5 and Reverse Engineer Anything. The company has an ongoing Cyber Verification Program, in which only approved entities get access to the full set of frontier models' cybersecurity capabilities.

#10347. Generators and Iterators in JavaScript: Lazy Data and Async Flows

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most JavaScript code loads data first and processes it afterward. That works for a list of ten items, but it falls apart when the list has a million entries, never ends, or arrives one network page at a time. Generators and iterators offer another approach: produce values only when someone asks for them. This article explains the iteration protocol, shows how generators build on it, and finishes with async generators for paginated data.

An iterator is any object with a next() method. Each call returns an object with two properties: value, the next item, and done, a boolean that becomes true when the sequence ends. An iterable is an object that hands out an iterator through a method keyed by Symbol.iterator. Arrays, strings, Maps and Sets are all iterables, which is why for...of, spread syntax and destructuring work on them.

Spread syntax calls [Symbol.iterator]() once, then calls next() until done is true. The code is correct but noisy. You manage the state yourself, and every new sequence needs the same scaffolding.

A generator function, declared with function*, returns an iterator without the manual bookkeeping. The yield keyword pauses the function and sends a value to the caller. The next call to next() resumes execution exactly where it stopped, with all local variables intact.

Calling countdown(3) does not run the body. It creates a generator object, and the body runs in slices as the consumer asks for values. Generator objects are iterable too, so spread and for...of work on them directly. The suspended state is the whole trick: the function body acts as a small state machine that the engine writes for you.

Values can also flow back in. The argument passed to next() becomes the result of the yield expression:

The first call to next() only runs the generator up to its first yield, so any argument passed to it is ignored. That detail trips up many developers.

Laziness is where generators earn their place. Array methods such as map and filter process the whole array at each step and allocate a new array each time. A generator pipeline handles one item at a time through the entire chain, which makes it possible to work with sequences that have no end:

The naturals generator never finishes, yet the pipeline completes because take stops asking after four results. No array of squares is ever built, and no number beyond 49 is computed.

There is a useful cleanup rule here. When a for...of loop exits early, through break, return or a thrown error, it calls the iterator's return() method. For a generator, that runs any finally blocks and ends the sequence. In the pipeline above, finishing take releases the generators upstream as well, so a generator that holds a file handle or a database cursor can close it inside a finally block.

Real applications spend more time waiting than computing, and async generators bring the same lazy model to asynchronous work. Declare one with async function* and consume it with for await...of. Each iteration waits for a promise to settle before the loop body runs.

A paginated API is a natural fit. Assume each response contains an items array and a nextUrl property that is null on the last page. This generator requests one page at a time and yields its items:

Once collectTitles has enough titles, the return statement ends the loop, which calls return() on the async generator. No further requests are made. Without a generator you would write a recursive function or a manual loop with its own stopping logic, and callers would have no say over the pace.

Async iteration also suits streams. In Node.js, readable streams are async iterable, so for await...of lets you process a large file chunk by chunk instead of holding all of it in memory.

Iterators define how to walk a sequence, generators make writing them painless, and async generators extend the same idea to data that arrives over time. Start small: replace one function that builds a large intermediate array with a generator, or one manual pagination loop with an async generator. The pull-based model keeps memory use predictable and gives the consumer control over how much work gets done.

#10346. PRX Part 3 — Training a Text-to-Image Model in 24h!

In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models. We tried to evaluate each idea in isolation, measuring throughput, convergence speed, and final image quality, and tried to understand what actually moves the needle.

In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:

What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?

Instead of optimizing one dimension at a time, we’ll stack the most promising ingredients together and see how far we can push performance under a strict compute budget.

To make things concrete, we’re doing a 24-hour speedrun:

This is very far from the early diffusion days, where training competitive models could cost millions of dollars. The goal here is to demonstrate how much the field has evolved and how far careful engineering can take you in just a single day of training.

This speedrun is not just a fun experiment. It will likely serve as the foundation for our large-scale training recipe going forward.

Alongside the results, we’re also open-sourcing our code (Github link), which contains:

So you can reproduce, modify, and extend everything yourself.

Now let’s walk through what went into this 24h run.

We use the x-prediction formulation from Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise [Li and He, 2025]. As seen in Part 2, this enables training directly in pixel space and eliminates the need for a VAE altogether. We use a patch size of 32 and use a 256-dimensional bottleneck in the initial token projection layer. This design keeps the sequence length under control, making pixel-space training computationally manageable even at higher resolutions.

(512/32)2=256 (512 / 32)^2 = 256 (512/32)2=256

(1024/32)2=1024 (1024 / 32)^2 = 1024 (1024/32)2=1024

Instead of following the usual 256px → 512px → 1024px schedule, we start directly at 512px and then fine-tune at 1024px.

With controlled token counts and modern hardware, pixel-space training is no longer prohibitive. It is simply a cleaner and more direct formulation.

One very nice side effect of predicting x0x_0x0​ directly in pixel space is that we can reuse a whole toolbox from classical computer vision.

When your model outputs latents, perceptual supervision becomes awkward. You either have to decode back to pixels or define losses in a learned latent space that may or may not align with human perception. Once you predict pixels directly, everything becomes straightforward again. You can plug in perceptual losses exactly as they were originally designed.

We take inspiration from the paper PixelGen: Pixel Diffusion Beats Latent Diffusion with Perceptual Loss [Ma et al.], where the authors introduce additional perceptual objectives on top of the diffusion loss. They show that adding perceptual signals can noticeably improve convergence speed and final visual quality.

For this 24h run, we add two auxiliary losses:

The idea is simple: In addition to the standard flow matching objective, we encourage the predicted clean image to match the target image in a perceptual feature space. LPIPS captures low-level perceptual similarity, while DINO features provide a stronger semantic signal.

We keep the same overall idea as the paper, but we tweaked a few details. In our experiments, we empirically found that it worked better to:

These are small implementation details, but in our setting they consistently gave better results.

We used a weight of 0.1 for the LPIPS loss and 0.01 for the DINO perceptual loss, matching the values recommended in the original paper.

These losses are lightweight compared to the main transformer forward pass, and in our setup they add only a small overhead while providing a consistent quality boost.

To make each step cheaper, we use token routing with TREAD [Krause et al., 2025]), which randomly selects a fraction of tokens and lets them bypass a contiguous chunk of transformer blocks, then re-injects them later so nothing is dropped.

We picked TREAD over SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) mostly for simplicity, and because the extra complexity of SPRINT did not feel worth the fairly small additional compute savings in our setting (sequence length 64 vs. 128 with TREAD at 512px).

Following the TREAD recipe, we route 50% of the tokens from the 2nd block to the penultimate block of the transformer.

Routed models can look worse under vanilla CFG, especially when undertrained, so we implemented a simple self-guidance scheme inspired by Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025), which guides using a dense vs. routed conditional prediction instead of relying on an unconditional branch.

We used REPA [Yu et al., 2024] for representation alignment.

For the teacher, we went with DINOv3 [Siméoni et al. 2025] since it gave the best quality improvements in our previous experiments.

Concretely, we apply the alignment loss once,at the 8th transformer block with a loss weight of 0.5.

Since we combine REPA with TREAD routing, we only compute the alignment loss on the non-routed tokens, meaning the tokens that actually go through the blocks where we apply the loss. This keeps the REPA signal consistent and avoids comparing features for tokens that skipped the computation path.

We used the Muon optimizer, using the FSDP implementation from muon_fsdp_2, since it showed a clear improvement over Adam in our previous runs.

Muon is only applied to 2D parameters (basically matrices). Everything else (biases, norms, embeddings, etc.) is optimized with Adam, which is why the config has two parameter groups.

We trained on three publicly available synthetic datasets:

The schedule is basically: go fast at 512, then sharpen at 1024:

We also keep an EMA of the weights for sampling and eval:

Below are the evaluation curves we tracked throughout the run and a few sample grids from the final checkpoint:

For a one day training run, this is already a pretty solid place to be. The model is not flawless yet (you can still spot some texture glitches, occasional weird anatomy, and it can get a bit shaky on very hard prompts), but it is clearly usable. Prompt following is strong, the overall aesthetic is consistent, and the 1024 stage mostly does what we want: sharpen details without breaking composition.

The key takeaway is that we're very close. The remaining issues look more like undertraining artifacts and limited data diversity than signs of a structural flaw in the recipe. The failure modes are consistent with what you’d expect from a model that simply hasn’t seen enough varied data yet. With more compute and broader coverage, this exact setup should continue improving in a fairly predictable way.

Zooming out, this speed run also highlights how far diffusion training has come. By combining pixel-space training, efficient routing, representation alignment, and lightweight perceptual guidance, you can now get a meaningful model in about a day on a budget that would have sounded unrealistic not that long ago.

This 24h run is just a starting point, not the finish line. Next, we will keep pushing the same recipe with a bit more scale and iterate on the dataset mix and captioning.

All the code and configs behind this speedrun, as well as the full experimental framework used throughout Part 1 and Part 2, are available in the PRX repository: https://github.com/Photoroom/PRX.

While we don’t redistribute the exact training datasets used in this run, the pipeline is fully configurable and designed to be easily adapted to your own data. You can plug in different datasets, tweak individual components (TREAD, REPA, perceptual losses, Muon, etc.), and run controlled experiments with minimal friction. Our goal is to make this a practical playground for fast diffusion research, and we hope the community will use it to explore, benchmark, and iterate on these techniques in their own setups.

If you made it this far, thank you for reading. We would also love to have you join our Discord community, where we share PRX progress and results, and discuss anything diffusion and text-to-image related.

Goodbye for now, and stay tuned for the next round of experiments! 🚀

This speedrun was inspired by several recent efforts exploring fast and low-cost training of diffusion models. If you're interested in speedrunning text-to-image models, we encourage you to check out the following works:

24 hours is very impressive, but looking at 32 H200 makes it make a bit more sense xD. Super cool that you used Muon! And, are you planning on releasing the re-captioned brivangl/midjourney-v6-llava?

Yeah, definitely not possible on consumer hardware… yet :D That’s also why we added the $1500 tag.

Regarding releasing the captions, we hadn’t really thought about that. If you think it would be valuable for the community, we can work on releasing them as well.

Hi, this article is very inspiring.I'd like to get your thoughts on the perceptual loss. During a research internship on (raw) image restoration - and trying to explore the perception/distortion tradeoff , I did a few attempts at VGG and Dino loss aswell. I always ended up with checkerboard patterns (no matter vgg or dino). If you look at the original paper from Johnson , it's full of these artifacts.Did you face any such issue or can share useful insights about that topic ?

I don’t think we really observed such artifacts, or at least not due to LPIPS. We did see something similar without LPIPS when using JIT on undertrained models, but I don’t think we observe them anymore. It might simply be because the model had not converged yet.One situation where we started to observe checkerboard patterns was during reward alignment with GRPO or SRPO on one of these models. In that case the artifacts were much more noticeable, but I don’t think they were related to LPIPS since we were not using it at the time.What type of model were you using?

Rosstat acknowledged suffering cyberattacks but denied leaked data claims.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) admitted that its servers were hit by coordinated cyberattacks between October 29 and 31. However, it denied claims that tens of terabytes of data had been leaked, as asserted by hack groups like the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow. Rosstat stopped publishing annual cause-of-death statistics in 2024, but the hackers say that the huge new 23TB data haul includes data on Russian wartime losses marked “for official use only,” reports The Moscow Times. A new chart shared by the hack groups using the data suggests that as many as 50,000 Russian soldiers are killed every month.

Rosstat is very much like the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics in the United States, or the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in the UK. It isn’t a big juicy military infrastructure target, but if accurate war casualty figures can come from the claimed exfiltrated data haul, then it would be a considerable win for Ukraine and its supporters.

Today @cpartisans and SilentCrow took down Russia's Federal State Statistics Service — the nerve center behind every socioeconomic number this regime produces. Full breakdown below 👇 https://t.co/wUKfyUi6y6November 1, 2026

As we mentioned in the intro, both the Belarusian CyberPartisans and Silent Crow claim to have snagged lots of sensitive data from the Russian government thanks to this breach. The former’s tweet includes evidence and a breakdown. “Entire IT infrastructure wiped: Domain controllers, databases, servers, virtualization, document workflow, workstations, admin consoles, VPN,” notes a follow-up post about the Rosstat hack attack. “Systems destroyed: STATEK, CSOD, Demography, SED, ESSO, OFSN, internal employee surveillance, StatRegister, websites and more.”

This is a developing story with the Belarusian CyberPartisans promising to share more sensitive information from Rosstat after they have picked through it. The Rosstat website was reportedly defaced with hacker messages and logos. Rosstat remains inaccessible at the time of writing.

We spotted an interesting graphic shared by the Belarusian CyberPartisans, which included the Silent Crow logo. A chart indicates that over the last two years, between 25,000 and 50,000 Russian soldiers were killed every month. The October 2026 figure is just a smidgen under 50,000, if this data leak news is genuine.

These same hacking groups have claimed responsibility for the likes of the disruptive Aeroflot IT systems hack, and a state real estate company hack with two billion records, both in 2025. “Both groups are designated as extremist and banned in Russia,” notes the report.

#10344. Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster

Last December, we announced preview of MCP support in Apigee: the ability to turn the APIs you already have, secured, governed and cataloged into tools that AI agents can discover and call, without writing code or standing up MCP servers of your own. The response from customers was immediate and so was the first question back: “can I have this where my runtime actually lives?”

For many Apigee customers, the runtime does not live on Google-managed infrastructure by accident. It lives in their own data center, in a colocation facility, or in another public cloud because a regulator requires it, because the systems of record are three racks away, or because a multi-cloud estate is simply the reality of the business. Those customers were not asking whether they wanted agentic access to their APIs. They were asking whether they could get it without moving the runtime.

And now they can. With Apigee hybrid 1.17.0, released on September 14, 2026, Model Context Protocol support is available in Apigee hybrid and the MCP data plane runs inside your own Kubernetes cluster.

The conceptual model is the one we shipped on Apigee, unchanged. You describe your API with an OpenAPI 3.0.x specification and create an MCP Discovery Proxy from it. Every operation in that spec becomes an MCP tool. Agents talk to the endpoint over JSON-RPC using tools/list to discover what is available and tools/call to invoke it and Apigee handles the protocol and the transcoding. You do not write MCP server code and you do not operate an MCP server as a separate piece of software with its own lifecycle.

What changes in hybrid is where the work happens. In Apigee hybrid, the MCP data plane runs inside your own Kubernetes cluster. The Apigee control plane generates MCP tool configuration from your OpenAPI Specification, your cluster fetches that configuration periodically and MCP request traffic never leaves the cluster. The diagram below shows where the MCP data plane runs in each deployment model.

Two properties of that architecture are worth stating plainly because they are the ones your security review team will ask about.

MCP request traffic stays inside your cluster. An agent's tools/call request is received, authorized and proxied to your backend entirely within your own infrastructure. No MCP request or response crosses the boundary to Google Cloud at request time.

Configuration is pulled, not pushed. A sidecar alongside the MCP data plane (from within your cluster) reaches out to fetch the tool configuration derived from your spec. The Apigee control plane (in Google Cloud) never initiates a connection into your cluster, which means MCP requires no inbound path from Google into your network.

MCP is an optional feature in Apigee hybrid and is not enabled by default. Enabling it is a Helm operation on a cluster already running Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 or later. Steps to do this are as follows.

Set the top-level enableMcpServer: true key in your overrides.yaml, then upgrade the apigee-operator chart first and the apigee-org chart second. The order matters. The operator chart owns the schema for the new MCP resources and upgrading in the wrong order produces a successful upgrade with no MCP pods. There is also a one-time, per-organization grant that adds the apigee-watcher identity to your organization's control plane access, so the sidecar can retrieve configuration. Defaults are sensible out of the box. Two MCP replicas, autoscaling to ten. Rolling back is the same field set to false and a single chart upgrade.

A few things to plan for before you schedule the change. Enabling or disabling MCP triggers a staged canary release of runtime pods, so run it in an approved maintenance window. The public documentation here describes how to enable MCP in an existing Apigee hybrid cluster.

Your MCP proxy is exposed as a single endpoint. Every agent request, whatever tool it invokes, arrives at the same /mcp path. Apigee tags each of those requests with the name of the tool that was called, so API insights can break that one endpoint out by tool and show which tools your agents actually used, how often and over what period. The screenshot below shows API insights, including requests to the MCP proxy (mcp) and also see individual tools (as API proxies mcp-healthcare, mcp-petstore, mcp-statuscode) response time and tps. See public documentation on monitoring and analyzing mcp traffic with Apigee API insights here and here on how to use the API insights dashboard.

We also have a view of tools being called in the tool performance tab within API insights below.

An MCP tool call crosses an AI client, Apigee and your backend. Today each of those is its own island of logs, so the question platform teams actually ask “where did the time go?” has no single answer.

The snippet below is an example mcp tools call request from an AI client. The curl request below allows for end to end tracking of the request, when distributed trace is enabled in Apigee with OTEL.

The same call as orchestrated by distributed trace in Google CloudTrace shows the calls in its entirety in one global view. (Assumption is all services (Apigee/Non-Apigee) in the chain report to the same Google CloudTrace)

MCP clients carry W3C trace context inside the JSON-RPC _meta field, which a conventional REST backend has no idea how to read. Apigee extracts it and forwards it as ordinary traceparent and tracestate headers, so instrumented services downstream join the trace without code changes. Three things follow: a single trace ID spanning the AI client, the Apigee proxies and backend execution; backends that participate without recoding and less noise, because the gateway can forward context in passthrough mode rather than emitting infrastructure spans of its own which also trims trace ingestion cost.

The ecosystem is converging on the same idea. SEP-2028, an open proposal in the MCP community, aims to standardize _meta-to-header forwarding of W3C trace context standard behavior for MCP servers.

The OpenTelemetry path that carries W3C trace context is available in Apigee today.

MCP support is available now in Apigee hybrid 1.17.0. Start with the MCP in Apigee overview for the architecture, Enable MCP in Apigee hybrid for the Helm procedure and the MCP quickstart to get a first tool answering an agent.

#10341. Introducing Modular Diffusers - Composable Building Blocks for Diffusion Pipelines

Modular Diffusers introduces a new way to build diffusion pipelines by composing reusable blocks. Instead of writing entire pipelines from scratch, you can mix and match blocks to create workflows tailored to your needs! This complements the existing DiffusionPipeline class with a more flexible, composable alternative.

In this post, we'll walk through how Modular Diffusers works — from the familiar API to run a modular pipeline, to building fully custom blocks and composing them into your own workflow. We'll also show how it integrates with Mellon, a node-based visual workflow interface that you can use to wire Modular Diffusers blocks together.

Here is a simple example of how to run inference with FLUX.2 Klein 4B using pre-built blocks:

You get the same results as with a standard DiffusionPipeline, but the pipeline is very different under the hood: it's composed of flexible blocks — text encoding, image encoding, denoising, and decoding — that you can inspect directly:

Each block is self-contained with its own inputs and outputs. You can run any block independently as its own pipeline, or add, remove, and swap blocks freely — they dynamically recompose to work with whatever blocks remain. Use .init_pipeline() to convert blocks into a runnable pipeline, and .load_components() to load the model weights.

For more on block types, composition patterns, lazy loading, and memory management with ComponentsManager, check out the Modular Diffusers documentation.

Modular Diffusers really shines when creating your own blocks. A custom block is a Python class that defines its components, inputs, outputs, and computation logic — and once defined, you can plug it into any workflow.

Here's an example block that extracts depth maps from images using Depth Anything V2.

Let's use this block with Qwen's ControlNet workflow. Extract the ControlNet workflow and insert the depth block at the beginning:

Blocks in a sequence share data automatically: the depth block's control_image output flows to downstream blocks that need it, and its image input becomes a pipeline input since no earlier block provides it.

You can publish your custom block to the Hub so anyone can load it with trust_remote_code=True. We've created a template to get you started — check out the Building Custom Blocks guide for the full walkthrough.

The DepthProcessorBlock from this post is published at diffusers/depth-processor-custom-block — you can load and use it directly:

We've published a collection of ready-to-use custom blocks here.

ModularPipeline.from_pretrained works with any existing Diffusers repo out of the box, but Modular Diffusers also introduces a new kind of repo: the Modular Repository.

A modular repository is able to reference components from their original model repos. For example, diffusers/flux2-bnb-4bit-modular contains a quantized transformer and loads the remaining components from the original repo.

Modular repositories can also host custom pipeline blocks as Python code and visual UI configurations for tools like Mellon — all in one place.

The community has already started building complete pipelines with Modular Diffusers and publishing them on the Hub, with model weights and ready-to-run code.

Teams can build novel architectures, package them as blocks, and publish the entire pipeline on the Hub for anyone to use with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained.

Check out the full collection of community pipelines for more.

💡 Mellon is in early development and not ready for production use yet. Consider this a sneak peek of how the integration works!

Mellon is a node graph interface integrated with Modular Diffusers. If you're familiar with node-based tools like ComfyUI, you'll feel right at home — but there are some key differences:

This integration is possible because every block exposes the same properties (inputs, intermediate_outputs, expected_components). This consistent API means Mellon can automatically generate a node's UI from any block definition and compose blocks into higher-level nodes.

For example, diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular contains a pipeline definition, component references, and a mellon_pipeline_config.json — all in one repo. Load it in Python with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular") or in Mellon to create either a single-node or multi-node workflow.

Here's a quick example. We add a Gemini prompt expansion node — hosted as a modular repo at diffusers/gemini-prompt-expander-mellon — to an existing text-to-image workflow:

Gemini expands your short prompt into a detailed description before generating the image. No code, no configuration — just a Hub repo id.

This is just one example. For a detailed walkthrough, check out the Mellon x Modular Diffusers guide. You can also check out this video!

Modular Diffusers brings the composability and flexibility the community has been asking for, without compromising the features that make Diffusers powerful. It's still early — we want your input to shape what comes next. Give it a try and tell us what works, what doesn't, and what's missing.

Thanks to Chun Te Lee for the thumbnail, and to Poli, Pedro, Lysandre, Linoy, Aritra, and Steven for their thoughtful reviews.

This is such a well written blog post! Thanks to the diffusers team for blessing us with this.

Google has updated its Android distribution numbers with the latest update showing that Android 17 is on just 1% of devices, while Android 16 now makes up the biggest slice of the pie.

Updated as of October 19, Google’s latest Android distribution numbers offer a peek into the rollout speed of Android 17. Having released to Pixel phones in June, the update has been available for roughly four months.

Google secures approval for its Minnesota data center despite local protests, lawsuits, and power supply concerns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google has secured approval for a proposed data center in Hermantown, Minnesota, following a unanimous vote by the city council, MPR News reports. The decision, reached on Friday, October 30, clears a major hurdle for the company following at least two postponed meetings and hours of public opposition, though the project still faces lawsuits and a separate inquiry into its electricity supply. The proposed development could cover just over 200 acres in a rural residential area outside Duluth with three data center buildings spanning approximately 1.66 million square feet.

The council approved a development agreement, a special use permit, and provisions for decommissioning the site if construction is abandoned or the facility eventually closes. The meeting, which was capped at 85 people and offered a livestream, ended shortly before midnight, with some criticizing the attendance restriction. Council member John Geisler, however, clarified the move, noting that the decision concerned local land use application rather than the wide debate over artificial intelligence or big technology companies.

“What we've done tonight is not about AI. It's not about big tech. It's not about software. It's about a project here in Hermantown, a land use application, and agreements that are associated with that,” Geissler said.

The approval comes at a hefty price for Google, with the company being forced to make several changes during the approval process. The company changed its initial plan of putting up four buildings to three, capped their height at 33 feet, and agreed to monitor nearby private wells —but each building would still be larger than six football fields. Google also agreed to withdraw an earlier request for up to $80 million in property tax breaks. The revised arrangement is now expected to generate about $3 million in annual property tax for the city, with a separate decommissioning agreement valued at $210 million in place.

Supporters point to those provisions as evidence that Google had responded to local concerns. Opponents, however, argue that the changes did not address the important questions of whether such a colossal development belongs in the area. The dispute echoes other data center battles within local communities, with Alabama residents being unable to halt a 50MW Bitcoin mining facility in August, despite local moratoriums, exposing gaps in the state's zoning rules. In September, a proposal for a 1,300-acre data center in Pennsylvania by NorthPoint Development also faced resistance despite its developer offering $10,000 to thousands of nearby households. Key issues raised mostly by residents in both cases have been about noise and water consumption by such facilities and property values.

It’s important to note, however, that Hermantown’s vote does not mean Google can immediately begin construction. Three lawsuits filed by The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy and Stop the Hermantown Data Center challenge the city’s zoning process and ownership of the land, and are also demanding the project’s environmental review. The project’s environmental needs are also another pain point, given it requires about 500 megawatts, comparable to the combined demands of homes in Minneapolis, St. Paul, Duluth, and Rochester, as per the Citizens Utility Board of Minnesota. Google still needs approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission on power consumption, despite its agreement with Minnesota Power.

The scale of demand is a recurring point of friction in data center proposals. Last year, the OpenAI Stargate facility in Michigan received approval for a 1.4-gigawatt power supply — construction, however, started in June 2026 despite objections from local residents. Google is also pursuing a separate data center project near Pine Island, close to Rochester. That proposal is now subject to a more extensive environmental review following a legal settlement.

#10334. Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens

Traditional OAuth bearer tokens operate on a "finders-keepers" model, making them vulnerable to Infostealer malware (e.g. RedLine, NodeStealer) and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks.

DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) is an application-layer OAuth 2.0 security profile (RFC 9449) that neutralizes token theft and replay attacks by cryptographically binding tokens to a client-generated asymmetric keypair at the application layer, ensuring that even if a token is stolen, it cannot be replayed without the corresponding private key.

This article is meant to inform you on where and how to adopt DPoP and describes Google's specific DPoP implementation. A DPoP adoption SKILL.md is also available to help implement DPoP.

Some optional features and implementation decisions in RFC 9449 are delegated to Google as an authorization provider. Google Identity, and its OAuth Platform, function as a developer-facing service where engineers implement OAuth 2.0 and cryptographic security controls like DPoP to protect API integrations. Separately, Google Workspace Context-Aware Access (CAA) leverages DPoP to secure enterprise AI workloads on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform by cryptographically validating agent identities at the Agent Gateway.

Google's OAuth Platform supports DPoP binding specifically for refresh tokens. This design choice reflects a pragmatic engineering tradeoff: by sender-constraining the long-lived refresh token, we neutralize the primary vector for persistent offline impersonation. Meanwhile, short-lived access tokens remain standard Bearer tokens, ensuring that high-QPS resource APIs do not incur the per-request asymmetric cryptographic verification overhead of DPoP. This approach delivers robust protection for your most sensitive credentials while maintaining the high performance and low latency of Google API integrations.

Unlike standard Bearer token flows, DPoP requires client-side cryptographic key generation, strict timestamp and nonce handling, specific claim computation (htm, htu, iat, jti), exact header construction, and DPoP proof JWT construction. These changes may introduce additional system constraints to support secure computation, handling, and storage.

The IETF’s Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security (RFC 9700) discusses sender-constrained refresh tokens. Additionally, the OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications IETF draft discusses three models: Backend-for-Frontend (BFF), Token-Mediating Backend, and Browser-based OAuth Client.

Following this guidance, Google recommends using DPoP to sender-contrain refresh tokens in these models.

Unlike transport-layer token binding (e.g., mTLS/RFC 8705) which often breaks or terminates at modern cloud proxies and load balancers, DPoP operates at the HTTP header level. This makes it highly resilient for complex, multi-hop environments, including emerging Model Context Protocol (MCP) and autonomous agent architectures.

A common question from security architects is: If DPoP is designed to sender-constrain tokens, why are Google's access tokens still standard Bearer tokens?

The answer lies in operational scaling and performance at Google's scale. Verifying asymmetric cryptographic signatures (such as ES256) requires significant CPU cycles. If every API call to high-throughput Google resource servers (like Gmail, Calendar, or Drive APIs) required verifying a DPoP proof, the compute overhead at the API Gateway layer would be massive, introducing measurable latency and scaling costs.

By constraining DPoP binding strictly to the refresh token, Google's architecture achieves a balance:

Long-Lived Credentials Protected: The highly sensitive, long-lived refresh token (which can be used to obtain new access tokens indefinitely) is cryptographically bound to the client's key pair. If exfiltrated, it is useless to an attacker.

High-Performance Serving: Short-lived access tokens (typically valid for 1 hour or less) remain standard Bearer tokens. This ensures that the vast majority of API requests incur zero cryptographic verification overhead, maintaining the high performance and low latency developers expect from Google APIs.

DPoP is a powerful tool for securing OAuth 2.0 tokens, but it is important to understand its boundaries.

As autonomous AI agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) architectures emerge, securing tool-use tokens becomes critical. While DPoP is highly resilient in single-hop client-to-server connections, multi-agent workflows (where Agent A delegates a task to Agent B, which calls Resource C) introduce delegation challenges.

In a multi-agent chain, Agent B cannot sign a DPoP proof on behalf of Agent A without access to Agent A's private key—and sharing private keys violates the core security principles of DPoP. Because Google's core consumer OAuth endpoint (oauth2.googleapis.com) does not support OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), developers building multi-agent or federated cloud workloads should consider Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS). By routing delegation through STS, the intermediate agent can exchange the upstream token for a new, short-lived federated token cryptographically bound to its own local key pair, preserving the sender-constrained security model across the entire agent chain without key exposure.

See our DPoP Adoption Guide, our DPoP adoption SKILL.md, and improve your platform security today.

Project takes a stock Qwen 3.5 4B and compiles a RISC-V CPU into its weights.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI engineer Divyansh Agrawal has revealed the Qwenputer. Described in its most basic terms, Qwenputer is an experimental blend of the stock Qwen 3.5 4B AI LLM with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU compiled and inserted directly into its weights. In use, Qwenputer can run processor arithmetic operations – or even run C and MicroPython code on its built-in CPU, eschewing any external runtime or tool use. Moreover, it can run Doom, albeit very slowly. You can see the Qwenputer running Doom on its RISC-V CPU by expanding the tweet below.

QWenputer by @divagr1925 is so cool! but... can it run DOOM? Ofc yes! E1M1 on the RISC-V CPU compiled into Qwen3.5-4B weights. will opensource too https://t.co/hEa46rD6CJOctober 29, 2026

The implementation of Qwenputer raises some interesting concepts and solutions. For example, the developer used Qwen’s Gated DeltaNet (GND) state as RAM, which Agrawal reckons is “a pretty neat trick.” They admit that using these ‘fast weights’ as RAM isn’t an original concept, but modifying Qwen 3.5 this way does seem to be a first.

Unlike traditional LLM creation, adding a ‘CPU’ doesn’t involve training. This RISC-V CPU implementation “is 11 transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, and none of their weights are learned: a compiler computes every one,” it is explained. Agrawal boasts that Qwenputer’s built-in CPU “passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error.”

The developer stresses that Qwen makes use of this ‘CPU’ to send instructions and read them back with no external tool or runtime calls. In practice, it works as intended. Use of the CPU inside Qwenputer provides exact calculations, overcoming the arithmetic weaknesses of many LLMs. Moreover, users can run code on the CPU inside the LLM, with C and MicroPython compatibility.

Not content with wedging a CPU into an LLM, Agrawal decided to also give it a filesystem. They describe this extension of the model as relatively trivial, since RAM is already in place. Indeed, the filesystem storage also uses the DeltaNet state. There are 1,024 slots holding up to 512 files. Moreover, this storage is persistent if you save the state at the end of a conversation with the LLM.

Due to its expanded resource use, Qwenputer has basically doubled the size of the underlying Qwen 3.5 4B LLM to almost 19GB. Thus, Agrawal recommends a workstation with 24GB of VRAM or more for testing Qwenputer in its current version. Efforts are being made to streamline coding in Qwenputer, as well as make it run faster.

The project is experimental. One gets the impression that Agrawal built Qwenputer primarily as an experiment to explore what is possible, rather than to solve a specific problem. Nevertheless, the creation of this custom LLM raises some interesting concepts and makes the mind wander regarding potential practical applications.

#10329. How Applicant Tracking Systems Read Resumes: 7 Checks Developers Should Make

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A resume that looks perfect on screen can look like a pile of scrambled text to a program. Applicant tracking systems (ATS) and hiring tools do not see your layout. They extract text from a file, guess where the sections are, and store what they find. If that step fails, the best experience in the world never reaches a human reader.

This matters whether you are sending your own resume or building a tool that processes thousands of them. This article walks through seven checks you can make with a few lines of Python, including one script you can run today.

A resume is a document with no guaranteed structure. One person writes "Work History", another writes "Experience", and a third uses a two-column layout that reads out of order. Any tool that processes resumes first has to turn this into predictable fields: contact details, sections, dates and skills.

Thinking in terms of a target schema helps. SitePoint's article on JSON schema design for document AI shows how the structure of the labels you define determines whether a document pipeline works. The same idea applies here: decide which fields you need before you write any extraction code.

Do not judge a resume by how it looks. Judge it by what comes out when you extract the text. SitePoint's walkthrough on building a JSON dataset from PDF documents describes a pipeline that extracts text from PDFs and then cleans up common extraction artifacts. That cleanup step exists because raw extraction is rarely tidy. Read the raw output first, and note what is broken.

PDF files store where characters are placed on a page, not what they mean. The pypdf documentation on extracting text from a PDF says this directly: there is no semantic layer, spacing is hard to get right because text is absolutely positioned, and pypdf is not OCR software, so it will never extract text from images.

Two practical results follow. A resume saved as a scanned image has no extractable text at all. And fancy layouts such as columns, text boxes and tables can come out in the wrong order.

Once you can extract text, a short script can catch the common failures. This one reads a PDF and reports whether it contains text, whether an email address is found, and which standard sections are missing:

Run it on a resume and look at the result. If has_text is false, the file is probably an image. If sections are missing, check whether your headings use unusual names. A passing result does not prove that every ATS will read the file the same way, but a failing result is a clear warning.

Different tools parse differently, so one script is only one opinion. A resume writing service such as ResumeCroc lists a free ATS resume checker among its tools, which is a quick way to see how another tool reads the same file. The linked page is a commercial service page, and every ATS behaves differently, so treat any checker as one data point and compare it with your own extraction results.

Most extraction problems come from layout. Single-column pages, standard headings, plain fonts and real text instead of images give parsers the best chance. Avoid putting contact details in headers or footers, since some tools skip them. If you are building a parser, test files with columns and tables on purpose so you know how your tool fails.

Create a folder of sample resumes: a clean one, a two-column one, a scanned one and one with unusual headings. Run your check against all of them whenever you change your parsing code. This turns "it seems to work" into something you can verify, and it makes regressions obvious.

Do all applicant tracking systems read PDFs the same way? No. Parsers differ in how they handle layout, headers and tables, so test more than one file format and more than one tool.

Is a Word file safer than a PDF? Not necessarily. Both can parse well or badly depending on layout. Test your own file instead of assuming.

Can a script guarantee my resume will pass an ATS? No. A script can find obvious problems, such as missing text or headings, but each hiring tool has its own rules.

Hiring tools read text, not layout. Define the fields you care about, extract the raw text first, understand what PDF extraction cannot do, automate basic checks, compare with an outside checker, keep formatting simple, and test against a small set of sample files. The script above is short, but it moves the question from "does it look right" to "what does a program actually see".

#10327. Apple finally has a touchscreen MacBook. Why now?

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

The Windows world has had touch for over a decade. Is Apple getting in the right way?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Last week, Apple finally brought two new display technologies to the MacBook Pro: OLED and touch. For the former, it was just a matter of time; Apple has been using OLED in the iPhone and Apple Watch for years, and also just brought it to the iPad Mini. But touch has never felt like a sure thing. While many of Apple's most successful products have relied on touch: the iPhone, the iPad, the Apple Watch, and some late-stage iPods all featured touchscreens. But until now, it never made its way to Apple's laptops.

Former Apple CEO Steve Jobs' words are infamous: "It's ergonomically terrible," he said of touchscreen laptops in 2010, describing how "your arm wants to fall off" due to fatigue. "Touch surfaces want to be horizontal," he added.

Since then, touchscreens have become ubiquitous on Windows PCs and Chromebooks. Outside of the Touch Bar, which was ultimately reversed because Mac users were not fans, Apple hasn't had a real touchscreen on the Mac.

That changed, as the company announced 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros with "PROLED XDR" displays with, yes, touch support. The devices are also lighter than existing MacBook Pros, have updated speaker systems, and, yes, are more expensive.

Apple eschewed touch on its laptops for years. But it seems, however, that at least some Mac owners disagreed.

"Apple tends not to move to a new technology until it can bring to market a differentiated product," Tom Mainelli, group vice president of device and consumer research at IDC, told Tom's Hardware. "Based on all the demos they are showing here in LA, the drive for 'why now' is because they see a desire for touch from creators who use the Mac."

He added: "The more business-focused answer is the company is creating further segmentation in a mature market, offering a new, more premium tier to its pro lineup."

There's one last uphill climb that the touchscreen on the new MacBook Pro faces: the price. After all, the touchscreen is debuting on just the new, redesigned 14- and 16-inch models.

In time, touch will likely fall down the stack, to the cheaper MacBook Pro models, the MacBook Air, and possibly even the Neo. You may see a touch iMac at some point. That will take time. After all, the Mac is just getting OLED, too. That means it's unlikely we'll see mass adoption of touch on the Mac anytime soon. It still has to reach the most popular devices, and even then, it has to coexist with the old standbys, keyboard and mouse.

You could trace the touchscreen laptop back to 2008's HP TouchSmart tx2, which had a swiveling screen. The real touch revolution started around two other releases: The Microsoft Surface Laptop RT and the release of Windows 8 in 2012, which had a touch-forward interface and led to a flood of touch laptops.

Windows 10 came and went with more touchscreens, and by the time of Windows 11's release in 2021, touchscreens largely became the default for Windows laptops. On all but the cheapest devices, I tend to assume a Windows notebook has a touchscreen.

On Chromebooks, the 2013 Chromebook Pixel was considered premium because of its touchscreen. In 2019, I reviewed the Samsung Chromebook Pro and Plus, as Google first experimented with Android apps in Chrome. I remember sitting there poking and prodding the device, thinking that "if Android apps are going to be on Chromebooks, every single one needs a touchscreen." I was seven years too early.

When Apple introduced the MacBook Neo earlier this year, it shocked the industry on price and performance. But it did cut some features, like a backlit keyboard. But some companies that made competitors, such as Dell with its XPS 13, made a point to add that not only did it have a backlit keyboard — it had a touchscreen. (HP also kept the touchscreen with its OmniBook 5. Acer did away with it on the Swift Air 14).

In an interview with Steven Levy at Wired, Apple's chief hardware officer Johny Srouji said that "Ten years is a very very long time," and said that a lot has changed, from display technology to custom silicon to software architecture, which now "met our bar." In the same interview, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, Greg Joswiak, explained that most creatives have an iPhone or iPad and find it natural: "There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch."

This might betray my age, but in general, outside of tablets and 2-in-1 laptops, I don't make a ton of use of touchscreens on computers. It hasn't bothered me once in the past five years that my personal MacBook Pro doesn't have a touchscreen. In general, I agree with Jobs; The ergonomics aren't great.

There are other reasons you might skip a touchscreen. For a long time, they were thought of as battery hogs. The digitizer can add extra weight or cost. And operating systems haven't been designed with touch in mind.

Windows 11 was supposed to be more designed for touchscreens, having taken cues from the unreleased Windows 10X, designed for touchscreens and foldables. But Windows is Windows, and the underlying OS still feels best with a keyboard and mouse.

One of the best operating systems I've seen for touch is Googlebook OS, if only because it's so based on Android 17 that some parts make more sense with a finger than a keyboard and mouse.

For macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple has added system gesture APIs to make apps more likely to support touch. Apple says its own apps are ready, and in its press release, listed a number of other apps like the Microsoft Office suite, Zoom, Notion, Da Vinci Resolve, Adobe Lightroom, Blender, and Algoriddim DJay Paro.

But it also didn't remove the keyboard and touchpad. It's a Mac with a touchscreen, but not touch-first.

For creative professionals who need true accuracy, specialty tablets that work as peripherals will still be king.

There's one last uphill climb that the touchscreen on the new MacBook Pro faces: the price. After all, the touchscreen is debuting on just the new, redesigned 14- and 16-inch models, starting at $2,899 for the 14-incher and $3,399 for the 16-inch models, respectively.

In time, touch will likely fall down the stack to the cheaper Pros, the MacBook Air, and possibly even the Neo. You may see a touch iMac at some point. That will take time. After all, the Mac is just getting OLED, too.

That means it's unlikely we'll see mass adoption of touch on the Mac anytime soon. It still has to reach the most popular devices, and even then, it has to coexist with the old standbys, keyboard and mouse.
